questions.stem: A customer support director is launching a Claude-powered chat assistant on the company website. To keep satisfaction scores high, the director proposes giving the assistant a friendly human name, a stock photo of a smiling agent, and a script that never mentions AI, because early testers rated 'human' replies more warmly. Which approach is MOST appropriate before launch?

options.text: Keep the human persona but add a line about AI assistance to the website's terms of service page.
Keep a friendly name if wanted, but clearly tell users at the start of each chat that they are talking to AI.
Keep the persona as tested, and have the assistant admit it is AI only if a customer asks it directly.
Drop the assistant entirely and keep all website support with human agents to avoid any disclosure issue.

questions.explanation: A friendly name and tone are fine, but hiding that the assistant is AI is not. Customers who believe a person is replying are being deceived, and they may share information or make decisions differently because of that belief. Clearly disclosing at the start of the conversation that users are chatting with an AI is the baseline for customer-facing AI, and it does not preclude a warm experience — it keeps the service while respecting customers' right to know who, or what, they are talking to.

whyWrong.A: Terms of service are not read at chat time and are not part of the conversation. A customer chatting with a named 'agent' would still reasonably believe a person is replying, so the deception remains.
whyWrong.C: Disclosing only when asked still relies on deceiving everyone who does not think to ask. The disclosure has to come first, not on request.
whyWrong.D: Abandoning the assistant is an over-correction. A responsible route exists: disclose clearly and keep the service.

questions.mindset: People have a right to know when they are talking to AI; tell them up front, then help them well.

questions.stem: An accounts-payable team uses Claude to pre-check supplier invoices against purchase orders and flag mismatches. Six months in, an audit shows that reviewers approved every one of Claude's 'no issues found' results, often within seconds, and two duplicate payments slipped through. The finance manager wants to keep the time savings but restore genuine human oversight. Which TWO actions are MOST effective? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have reviewers fully re-check a random sample of 'no issues' invoices each week and log what they find.
Ask Claude to add a confidence percentage to each result and only send low-confidence ones to reviewers.
Remove the human review step, since six months of agreement shows the pre-check is already reliable.
Add more invoice examples to Claude's instructions so it catches duplicates without needing reviewers.
Require reviewers to record which specific fields they compared before approving any high-value invoice.

questions.explanation: The problem is overreliance: reviewers stopped checking because the tool is usually right. Random sampling with logged findings measures real accuracy and keeps reviewers engaged, and requiring a short record of what was actually compared turns a rubber stamp back into a real check where the stakes are highest. Both keep humans accountable for payment decisions without discarding the efficiency gain — matching the safeguard to the risk instead of trusting the streak.

whyWrong.B: A model's self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal, and Claude can be confidently wrong. It moves the oversight decision back onto the model being overseen.
whyWrong.C: The audit already found duplicate payments. 'Reviewers always agreed' shows the reviews were not happening, not that the tool is flawless.
whyWrong.D: Better instructions may improve the pre-check, but a prompt change is not oversight. Nobody would notice the next failure any faster.

questions.mindset: When approvals become automatic, oversight has quietly stopped; rebuild the check, don't trust the streak.

questions.stem: A consulting firm notices that its first-year analysts now produce polished market summaries with Claude, but in client meetings they struggle to explain the reasoning behind their own slides. The practice lead wants analysts to keep using Claude while still building the core analytical skills the role needs. What is the BEST change?

options.text: Have analysts write their own first-pass analysis, then use Claude to critique it and suggest gaps before finalizing.
Ban Claude for first-year analysts until they have two years of experience doing the work entirely by hand.
Ask Claude to add a detailed explanation section to every summary so analysts can read it before meetings.
Assign a senior partner to present all client findings so the analysts' explanation gaps never reach clients.

questions.explanation: This is a deskilling risk. Putting the analyst's own thinking first and using Claude as a critic or coach keeps the core skill in practice while still getting the quality boost. The analyst can then defend the work in the meeting because the key judgments are theirs, not the model's.

whyWrong.B: A blanket ban throws away a useful tool and is out of step with how the firm now works. A proportionate change in how Claude is used solves the problem.
whyWrong.C: Reading an AI-written explanation before a meeting is memorizing, not reasoning. The analysts still never practice forming the analysis themselves.
whyWrong.D: Hiding the gap from clients leaves the real problem in place. The analysts never develop, and accountability for the work stays unclear.

questions.mindset: Use Claude to sharpen your thinking, not to replace the thinking you are paid to do.

questions.stem: A secondary-school teacher uses Claude to draft end-of-term report comments from a spreadsheet of each student's name, grades and teacher notes. Reading the drafts side by side, she notices that students with almost identical grades and notes get noticeably different tone: some are described as 'confident leaders' and others as 'well-behaved and quiet', in a pattern that seems to follow the students' names. She wants fair comments without giving up the time savings. Which TWO steps should she take? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add a sentence to the prompt asking Claude to be completely unbiased and to treat all students equally.
Switch to the most capable Claude model, since a stronger model will not show this kind of bias.
Generate comments from the grades and notes with student names replaced by neutral codes, adding names afterwards.
Keep the drafts but add a note to parents that comments were AI-generated and may contain errors.
Compare comments for students with matching evidence and edit any differences the evidence does not justify.

questions.explanation: Claude can reflect biases, including stereotypes cued by names, so outputs need to be checked for them rather than assumed fair. Removing the irrelevant cue (names) from the input takes away one route for bias, and comparing outputs for students who should be treated alike is a direct check that catches whatever slips through. The teacher stays responsible for the final comments that go home.

whyWrong.A: Asking the model to be unbiased is a vague instruction with no way to confirm it worked. The comparison check is what actually reveals unfair differences.
whyWrong.B: No model is guaranteed free of bias. Changing model without changing the inputs or the review process does not address the cause.
whyWrong.D: A disclaimer does not make unfair comments fair. Parents would still receive uneven descriptions of their children.

questions.mindset: Remove cues that shouldn't matter, then check that like cases get like treatment.

questions.stem: A freelance consultant sent a client a market-entry report that Claude helped draft. The client later finds that one growth statistic, which drove a key recommendation, does not appear in any of the cited sources. The client asks the consultant to explain. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Explain that the figure came from Claude, so the error belongs to the AI tool rather than to the consultant.
Ask Claude to find a different source that supports the original figure and send that to the client instead.
Point out that the report's footer said AI was used, so the client should have verified the numbers themselves.
Own the error, correct the figure and recommendation, and add source verification to the drafting process.

questions.explanation: The person who sends the work owns it. Claude can produce confident, plausible-looking figures that are not real, which is exactly why claims that drive decisions must be verified against authoritative sources before — and here, after — they are shared. Taking responsibility, fixing the substance, and closing the process gap is the accountable response.

whyWrong.A: Blaming the tool does not move responsibility. The consultant chose to send the report, and 'the AI said so' is not a defense.
whyWrong.B: Hunting for a source to fit a number reverses good practice. It risks a second fabrication and does not fix the recommendation.
whyWrong.C: Disclosing AI use is good practice, but it never shifts the duty to check facts onto the reader.

questions.mindset: You signed it, you own it: AI help never moves accountability off the human.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator has a competitor's paid industry whitepaper, downloaded under a license for internal reading only. Her manager asks her to upload it to Claude and have Claude 'reword it enough' to publish as the company's own thought-leadership piece next week. What should she do?

options.text: Upload it and ask Claude to change at least half the wording so the result counts as an original work.
Upload it but have Claude cite the competitor in a footnote so the company is protected from complaints.
Explain the concern, and use Claude to build an original piece from the company's own data and public sources.
Paste the whitepaper in short sections across separate chats so no single chat holds the full document.

questions.explanation: Rewording someone else's licensed work and presenting it as your own raises both intellectual property and honesty problems, and the license itself limits how the file may be used — an inappropriate-use and data-sensitivity issue, not a prompting issue. Claude is still useful here: it can help build genuinely original thought leadership from material the company has the right to use, with public sources properly attributed.

whyWrong.A: Changing a share of the words does not make borrowed ideas and structure original. It is still passing off someone else's work.
whyWrong.B: A footnote does not grant rights the license withholds, and publishing a reworded copy as thought leadership is still misleading.
whyWrong.D: Splitting the upload across chats changes nothing about the rights or the honesty problem. It is a workaround, not a safeguard.

questions.mindset: Claude should help you create original work, not disguise someone else's.

questions.stem: A small charity's fundraising officer wants Claude to write five heartfelt first-person letters 'from' children the charity supports, describing how donations changed their lives, for the year-end appeal. No such letters exist, and the officer would add stock photos of children. The officer argues the stories are 'typical of our work'. What is the MOST appropriate way forward?

options.text: Use Claude to help shape real stories that beneficiaries or families have consented to share, edited honestly.
Have Claude write the letters but change the children's names so no real child can be identified from them.
Write the letters with Claude and add small print saying some details have been changed for privacy reasons.
Have Claude write the letters as long as each one reflects outcomes the charity has actually achieved.

questions.explanation: Inventing first-person testimonials and presenting them as real is deceptive to donors, however typical the stories feel. Claude can still help: it can turn genuine, consented stories into compelling letters while keeping them truthful. That respects both the donors and the people whose lives are described.

whyWrong.B: Changing names solves a privacy problem the letters don't have. The real problem is that the letters are made up and presented as genuine.
whyWrong.C: 'Details changed for privacy' implies the letters are real with small edits. That small print makes the deception worse, not better.
whyWrong.D: Real outcomes in aggregate do not make a fabricated first-person letter genuine. Donors would still be misled about who wrote it.

questions.mindset: Claude can make a true story compelling; it should not make a false story look true.

questions.stem: An online store is launching a new product with no customer reviews yet. The e-commerce manager asks Claude to generate twenty varied, realistic five-star reviews with different customer names to post on the product page until real reviews arrive. Which response is BEST?

options.text: Post the generated reviews but label the product page as 'early impressions' instead of 'customer reviews'.
Post only five of the generated reviews so the product page looks credible without seeming over-promoted.
Generate the reviews but base each one on real features of the product so nothing they say is untrue.
Decline fake reviews, and use Claude to draft a post-purchase email inviting real buyers to leave honest reviews.

questions.explanation: Reviews attributed to customers who don't exist are fabricated records that mislead shoppers, even when the product features they mention are real. The honest way to get the same benefit is to gather genuine reviews faster, and Claude can help with that outreach instead.

whyWrong.A: Renaming the section does not change the fact that invented customers are being presented as real people.
whyWrong.B: Posting fewer fake reviews is still posting fake reviews. Reducing the amount of deception does not make it acceptable.
whyWrong.C: Accurate features do not make the reviewers real. Shoppers are misled about who is vouching for the product.

questions.mindset: If it pretends a real person said it, don't generate it.

questions.stem: An operations analyst is entering her company's internal innovation award. The rules say each submission essay must be 'the entrant's own work', and say nothing explicit about AI. She has used Claude heavily to draft the essay and is unsure whether that is acceptable. What should she do?

options.text: Submit as is, because the rules do not mention AI and so any level of AI assistance is permitted.
Ask the award organizers how AI assistance is treated, and disclose or adjust her use to match their answer.
Ask Claude whether her essay still counts as her own work under the rules, and follow its assessment.
Rewrite the essay's wording herself so that AI detection tools are unlikely to recognize Claude's text.

questions.explanation: Where a submission must be the entrant's own work, heavy undisclosed AI drafting can misrepresent authorship. When the governing rules are silent, the honest route is to ask the people who set them, then disclose or adjust — the same way one would clarify any ambiguous organizational policy before acting. That keeps her entry fair to other entrants.

whyWrong.A: Silence in the rules is not permission. 'Own work' is the very requirement that heavy AI drafting may conflict with.
whyWrong.C: Claude cannot interpret or authorize the organizers' rules. Only the organizers can say what counts.
whyWrong.D: Rewording to avoid detection is concealment. It treats the problem as getting caught rather than being honest about authorship.

questions.mindset: When authorship matters and the rules are unclear, ask and disclose; never disguise.

questions.stem: An HR operations lead wants to export six months of employees' internal chat messages and have Claude score each named employee's 'engagement' and flag people who seem likely to resign, so managers can intervene early. Employees have not been told their messages would be analyzed this way. Leadership likes the idea because it is cheaper than a survey. What is the MOST appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Proceed, but ask Claude to avoid quoting any message directly in the scores it gives each employee.
Proceed with the analysis only for teams whose managers have specifically asked for the risk scores.
Proceed, but share the scores only with HR and not with line managers, to limit how widely they spread.
Don't profile individuals covertly; propose a transparent, anonymous engagement survey analyzed in aggregate.

questions.explanation: Scoring named employees on their emotional state and likely resignation, using private messages they never agreed to have analyzed this way, is covert profiling. It fails basic data-sensitivity, consent and fairness expectations, it can seed career-affecting judgments from shaky inferences, and it would destroy workplace trust if discovered — narrowing or relabeling the analysis does not satisfy those controls, just as telling a model 'don't retain this' would not. The legitimate goal of understanding engagement can still be met openly: an anonymous survey analyzed in aggregate gives leadership real signal without targeting individuals.

whyWrong.A: Suppressing quotes does not change what is being done: named people are covertly scored on private communications without their consent.
whyWrong.B: A manager's request is not the employees' consent. It narrows the scope but keeps the core problem intact.
whyWrong.C: Limiting who sees the scores still leaves named individuals profiled without their knowledge, with possible effects on their careers.

questions.mindset: Meet the business goal openly; don't profile people behind their backs.

questions.stem: A town council's communications officer uses Claude to summarize 2,400 public comments on a proposed bus route change. The summary will go to councillors before they vote. The first draft is clear but reads as if residents broadly support the change, and the officer worries that smaller groups, such as disabled residents who rely on the current stops, may be under-represented. Which TWO steps are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have Claude group comments by theme with counts and quotes, then check sampled raw comments against each theme.
Ask Claude to focus the summary on the most common opinions so that councillors get a short, decisive read.
Tell councillors in the briefing that the summary was AI-assisted and how staff checked it against the comments.
Let Claude decide which comments are relevant enough to include, since it can read all 2,400 consistently.
Switch to a more capable model and accept its summary, since it will weigh every viewpoint more fairly.

questions.explanation: Summaries can silently drop minority positions, and here that could shape a public decision. Structuring the output by theme with counts and verbatim quotes makes gaps visible and checkable — the same grounding-and-verify discipline recommended for long documents — and checking the themes against a sample of raw comments catches what the model missed. Telling decision-makers how the summary was produced and verified lets them weigh it appropriately and keeps the public process transparent.

whyWrong.B: Focusing on the majority is exactly how the needs of smaller groups disappear. It makes the fairness problem worse.
whyWrong.D: Handing relevance judgments to the model removes the human accountability that a public consultation requires.
whyWrong.E: A stronger model may summarize better, but nobody would know whether it was fair without a check against the source comments.

questions.mindset: When AI shapes a decision about people, make sure every affected voice is visible and the method is disclosed.

questions.stem: An operations manager used Claude to analyze staffing data and recommend closing one of three regional warehouses. In the leadership deck, the manager plans to present the recommendation as 'the AI's objective, data-driven answer', reasoning that executives will find it harder to argue with than a manager's view. What is the BEST way to present it?

options.text: Present it as the AI's objective answer, since it was produced from the company's own data with no edits.
Present it as the manager's recommendation, prepared with AI help, with the assumptions and limits stated.
Present the AI output and the manager's own view as two separate options and let executives choose between them.
Leave out any mention of AI so executives judge the recommendation purely on the numbers that are shown.

questions.explanation: AI output is not neutral or objective just because a machine produced it: it reflects the data, the framing and the prompt, and it can be wrong. Presenting it as the manager's recommendation, transparently prepared with AI help and with its assumptions and limits stated, keeps a human accountable for a decision that affects people's jobs and lets executives question it properly.

whyWrong.A: Calling it 'objective' uses AI as an authority to shut down debate. The analysis still rests on choices someone made and could be wrong.
whyWrong.C: Framing the AI as a separate voice avoids ownership. Someone still has to stand behind the recommendation and its assumptions.
whyWrong.D: Hiding AI involvement removes context executives may need to judge the analysis, and conflicts with transparency expectations.

questions.mindset: AI output is an input to your judgment, never a neutral authority to hide behind.

questions.stem: A public health outreach team uses Claude to translate a vaccination clinic flyer from English into four community languages. The English version was reviewed by a nurse, but nobody on the team reads the other languages, and the deadline is tight. What is the MOST responsible way to proceed?

options.text: Publish all four translations, since the English source has already been checked by a qualified nurse.
Ask Claude to translate each version back into English and publish if the back-translation matches.
Have a fluent speaker, ideally with health knowledge, check each translation before it is published.
Publish the flyer only in English so that no community receives information that has not been checked.

questions.explanation: Communities that rely on translated health information deserve the same accuracy as English readers. A reviewed source does not guarantee a correct translation, and a machine checking its own output is not reliable verification — so each version needs a qualified human review before publication. That is both a fairness and an accuracy safeguard for a high-stakes audience.

whyWrong.A: The nurse checked the English, not the translations. Errors introduced in translation would reach the communities least able to spot them.
whyWrong.B: Back-translation by the same model is a self-check. It can miss nuance and errors, and cannot replace a fluent human reviewer.
whyWrong.D: English-only is an over-correction that leaves those communities without the information at all, which is its own fairness harm.

questions.mindset: Every audience deserves the same level of checking, not just the one you can read.

questions.stem: A product team's UX lead asks Claude to create six customer personas for a budgeting app. All six come back as young, urban, salaried professionals, although the company's own data shows many customers are retirees and self-employed people with irregular income. The team wants personas they can rely on for design decisions. Which TWO actions are BEST? Choose TWO.

options.text: Accept the personas, since Claude reflects the typical users of budgeting apps across the whole market.
Give Claude the company's real customer segment data and ask for personas grounded in those segments.
Ask Claude to make the personas 'more diverse' without giving it any further information about customers.
Generate twenty more personas and keep the six that look most realistic to the design team members.
Label the personas as drafts and check them against real user interviews before using them for decisions.

questions.explanation: Generated personas can default to common patterns that leave out real groups, so outputs need to be checked against reality rather than accepted. Grounding the request in the company's actual segment data addresses the cause, and treating the output as a draft to validate against real users keeps synthetic personas from replacing the research they are meant to support.

whyWrong.A: The company's own data contradicts the personas. 'Typical' in general is not the same as accurate for this customer base.
whyWrong.C: 'More diverse' with no data produces tokenistic variety, not personas that match the real customers.
whyWrong.D: Generating more and keeping what 'looks realistic' simply filters by the team's own assumptions, which may share the same blind spot.

questions.mindset: Ground AI in your real people and validate it; don't let a plausible default stand in for them.

questions.stem: After reading about AI bias, a people-operations team lead tells her team to stop using Claude for all HR-related work. This includes reformatting the employee handbook, proofreading policy updates and drafting meeting agendas, none of which involve decisions about individuals. Which response BEST reflects responsible AI use?

options.text: Keep using Claude for low-risk HR writing, while keeping humans responsible for any decisions about people.
Support the ban, since any HR-related use of AI carries the same level of risk as decisions about staff.
Allow all HR uses again, including screening applicants, as long as Claude is told to be fair in each prompt.
Replace the ban with a rule that every HR document must carry a disclaimer stating that AI may be wrong.

questions.explanation: Responsible use is proportionate to risk. Formatting, proofreading and agendas carry little ethical risk, while decisions affecting individuals need human judgment and, often, extra review. Matching safeguards to actual risk keeps the benefit without ignoring the real concern behind the lead's worry.

whyWrong.B: Treating proofreading the same as decisions about people is an over-correction. It gives up useful work without reducing any meaningful risk.
whyWrong.C: This swings to the opposite extreme. Hiring decisions are high-risk, and a fairness instruction in a prompt is not a safeguard.
whyWrong.D: A blanket disclaimer is not review. It adds noise to low-risk documents and does nothing to protect people where it matters.

questions.mindset: Scale safeguards to the risk: light touch for formatting, human judgment for decisions about people.
